newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss experts split over central bank's next moves.
newsitem.headline: Swiss experts split over central bank's next moves.

text.p: Swiss interest rates continue steady but widespread speculation about the Swiss National Bank's (SNB) policy has led to a falling-out among economists trying to predict what it will do next.
Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) group economist Klaus Wellershof is ready to say the Swiss discount rate may rise late this year.
But some economists think it is too soon to start to talk about tightening. Others are looking in the opposite direction at the chances of a further easing.

The SNB's most recent change was on September 26 when it lowered its discount rate by half a percentage point to 1.00 percent, returning to the historic low maintained from February 1978 to November 1979.
Its aim was to boost the stagnant Swiss economy and weaken the Swiss franc. The bank has said since then that it welcomed the decline in the franc that took place in response to its easing.

Wellershof says he does not really believe the SNB will raise its discount rate until perhaps very late this year, if at all. He adds the discount rate has little real significance in terms of lending.
"I think the word tightening is a little strong. We think they will shift to a more neutral policy stance. The first wave of this would have no effect on money market rates," he said.
Credit Suisse First Boston has focused on chances for further SNB easing.

"We think the SNB will gradually bias money market rates towards the low end of the current money market range. We think that will generally help to support the entire yield curve moving down," said Adam Beaudin, one of CSFB's two main currency strategists.

He said CSFB did not think there was much chance of a rate increase this year. "If there is a surprise it is going to be a discount rate cut rather than any mention of higher rates. We think the economy is in worse shape than is generally believed."
At Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), senior economist Markus Allenspach said he sees money market conditions pretty much unchanged this year, albeit with a chance for lower money market rates.
"If anything, the SNB would bring short-term rates back to levels we saw in September," Allenspach said.
He said this could mean that three-month Euro Swiss rates, now at 1-5/8 percent, could drop back to 1-3/8 percent.
But if Switzerland reaches a bilateral trade agreement with the European Union sooner than expected -- he doesn't expect an agreement this year -- this could improve the economic outlook.
At the same time, he expected growth in the SNB's money supply aggregate, which was strong late last year, to slow as money is shifted from low-interest cash accounts to bonds.

Martin Leber, senior economist at Zuercher Kantonalbank, said that even if the Swiss economy does show signs of recovery, the SNB would be worried the Swiss franc could again appreciate if it raised rates.
"It is not enough to put the economy in stronger position. They must take care that the franc doesn't overvalue," he said, adding this would mean keeping the mark above 84.00 to 85.00 Swiss centimes.

He said a tightening appeared unlikely as long as German interest rates stayed low. German rates are expected to stay low as the country works to get its fiscal policy in shape for European monetary union this year.
He saw any chance of higher Swiss rates "only at the end of this year, at the earliest."
